docs.title: ABFML
docs.text:
ABFML (Apply, Build, Fit Machine Learning force field) is a Python-based package designed to simplify the development, screening, and tuning of new machine learning force field (MLFF) models.

Unlike tools that focus on a single model, ABFML is specifically intended for constructing and applying new MLFF models and descriptors. Its modular design simplifies operations, facilitates integration of training and simulation, and allows researchers to leverage existing MLFF models or develop and select models tailored to their specific problems.

Important

The project ABFML is licensed under GNU LGPLv3.0. If you use this code in any future publications, please cite the following references:

  • Xingze Geng, Jianing Gu, Gaowu Qin, Lin-Wang Wang,and Xiangying Meng. “ABFML: A problem-oriented package for rapidly creating, screening, and optimizing new machine learning force fields.”* J. Chem. Phys. 162, 052502 (2025)

In addition, please see this page for more citation details.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Rapid construction of MLFF models based on physical descriptors
  • Support for large-scale molecular dynamics via LAMMPS and ASE
  • Modular design for easy extension and research customization

docs.title: Easy Install
docs.text:
pip install abfml
For more details, check the Installation Guide and Tutorials.

docs.title: Command-Line Interface (CLI)
docs.text:
ABFML provides a command-line interface for quick model checking, training, and validation. You can display general help using: 

abfml --help

Check the validity and inference capability of a trained model. 

abfml check -m model.pt -d float32
- Purpose: Ensures the model file can be loaded and used for inference.

docs.title: train
docs.text:
Start training a machine learning force field model based on a configuration file. 

abfml train input.json
- Purpose: Launches the training process using parameters defined in input.json.

docs.title: valid
docs.text:
Validate a trained model using a test dataset. 

abfml valid -m model.pt -f "../data/test.extxyz" -n 10
- Purpose: Evaluates model performance with sp

docs.title: Help for Commands
docs.text:
Each command provides detailed parameter information using -h: 

abfml train -h
abfml valid -h
abfml check -h

docs.title: 1. Installing ABFML
docs.text:
To quickly get started with ABFML, set up an isolated Python environment and install the package.

# 1. Create a new conda environment
conda create -n abfml python=3.11

# 2. Activate the environment
conda activate abfml

# 3. Install ABFML

# Option 1: Install from source (recommended for development)
cd path/to/ABFML
pip install .

# Option 2: Install from PyPI (for general use)
pip install abfml

docs.title: 2. Installing ABFML-LAMMPS (Optional)
docs.text: This step is only required if you plan to run large-scale molecular dynamics simulations with LAMMPS using ABFML-generated force fields. For initial model development and testing, ABFML works directly with ASE and you can skip this section.

docs.title: 2.1 Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. LAMMPS Download and build LAMMPS for your platform: LAMMPS Official Website

  2. Libtorch Download the PyTorch C++ API (Libtorch). If your system's toolchain is older, use the Pre-cxx11 ABI version.

docs.title: 1. Copy ABFML files into LAMMPS
docs.text:
cp abfml/lmp/ABFML lammps/src
cp abfml/lmp/Makefile.mpi lammps/src/MAKE

docs.title: 2. Modify Makefile.mpi
docs.text:
Edit lammps/src/MAKE/Makefile.mpi to match your system paths for compilers and libraries: 

CCFLAGS += -I/PATH/libtorch/include/
CCFLAGS += -I/PATH/libtorch/include/torch/csrc/api/include/
CCFLAGS += -I/PATH/libtorch
LINKFLAGS += -L/PATH/libtorch/lib/ -ltorch -lc10 -ltorch_cpu

docs.title: 3. Build LAMMPS with ABFML
docs.text:
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/path/libtorch/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
cd lammps/src
make yes-abfml
make mpi

docs.title: 2.3 Running LAMMPS with ABFML
docs.text:
Example of using ABFML in an input script: 

pair_style abfml model.pt
pair_coeff * * 29 30
Here, element numbers (e.g., 29, 30) represent element types.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Ensure that the Libtorch version matches the PyTorch version used for training the ABFML model.
  • Always verify the correct LD_LIBRARY_PATH before running LAMMPS.

docs.title: FieldModel(type_map, cutoff, neighbor)
docs.text:
Bases: Module, ABC

Abstract base class for machine learning force field models.

FieldModel provides a standardized interface for implementing custom force field models within the ABFML framework. It handles the automatic computation of forces and virial tensors through automatic differentiation, allowing developers to focus on implementing the energy calculation logic.

The class manages the complete physics pipeline: - Neighbor list processing - Energy computation (via the abstract field method) - Automatic force derivation using PyTorch autograd - Virial tensor calculation

Subclasses must implement the field method to define the specific energy calculation for their force field model.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
• type_map : List[int] Mapping of atomic species to model indices. Each unique element type should have a corresponding integer in this list.

  • neighbor : Union[Dict[int, int], int] Maximum number of neighbors per atom. Can be either:

    • int: Global maximum for all atom types
    • Dict[int, int]: Type-specific maximums {type_id: max_neighbors}

  • cutoff : float Cutoff radius (in Angstroms) for neighbor search. Atoms beyond this distance are not considered neighbors.

Source code in abfml\core\model\method.py 
def __init__(self,
             type_map: List[int],
             cutoff: float,
             neighbor: Union[Dict[int, int],int]):

    super(FieldModel, self).__init__()
    self.type_map = type_map
    self.neighbor = neighbor
    self.cutoff = cutoff

docs.title: field(element_map, central_atoms, neighbor_indices, neighbor_types, neighbor_vectors, n_ghost)
docs.text:
Compute atomic energies and optionally forces for the force field model.

This abstract method must be implemented by all subclasses. It defines the core physics of your force field - how atomic environments are converted into energies (and optionally forces/virials).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
element_map : torch.Tensor Atomic numbers for each atom, shape [batch_size, n_atoms]. Use this to apply element-specific parameters in your model.

torch.Tensor

Type indices (not atomic numbers) for central atoms, shape [batch_size, n_atoms]. Indices into self.type_map. Use for type-dependent calculations.

torch.Tensor

Neighbor atom indices, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, max_neighbors]. Value -1 indicates padding (no real neighbor). Use with torch.gather to collect neighbor properties.

torch.Tensor

Neighbor type indices, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, max_neighbors]. Corresponds to neighbor_indices, giving type of each neighbor.

torch.Tensor

Relative positions, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, max_neighbors, 4]. Format: [distance, dx, dy, dz] - distance: ||r_j - r_i|| in Angstroms - dx, dy, dz: components of r_j - r_i vector Use distance for radial functions, components for angular terms.

int

Number of ghost atoms (periodic images) in the system. Usually can be ignored unless doing specialized handling.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Dict[str, torch.Tensor] Dictionary with the following keys:

**Required**:
- 'Etot' : torch.Tensor, shape [batch_size, 1]
    Total energy for each configuration in the batch.
    Must be provided and have correct shape.

- 'Ei' : torch.Tensor, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, 1]
    Per-atom energy contributions. Should sum to Etot.
    Must be provided and have correct shape.

**Optional** (provide only if computing analytically):

- 'Force' : torch.Tensor, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, 3]
    Atomic forces F = -dE/dr in Cartesian coordinates.
    If not provided, computed automatically via autograd.

- 'virial' : torch.Tensor, shape [batch_size, 3, 3]
    Virial stress tensor. Only relevant if providing Force.

- 'atomic_virial' : torch.Tensor, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, 9]
    Per-atom virial contributions (flattened 3x3 tensors).
Source code in abfml\core\model\method.py 
def field(self,
          element_map: torch.Tensor,
          central_atoms: torch.Tensor,
          neighbor_indices: torch.Tensor,
          neighbor_types: torch.Tensor,
          neighbor_vectors: torch.Tensor,
          n_ghost: int) -> Dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
    """
    Compute atomic energies and optionally forces for the force field model.

    This abstract method must be implemented by all subclasses. It defines the
    core physics of your force field - how atomic environments are converted
    into energies (and optionally forces/virials).

    Parameters
    ----------
    element_map : torch.Tensor
        Atomic numbers for each atom, shape [batch_size, n_atoms].
        Use this to apply element-specific parameters in your model.

    central_atoms : torch.Tensor
        Type indices (not atomic numbers) for central atoms, shape [batch_size, n_atoms].
        Indices into self.type_map. Use for type-dependent calculations.

    neighbor_indices : torch.Tensor
        Neighbor atom indices, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, max_neighbors].
        Value -1 indicates padding (no real neighbor). Use with torch.gather
        to collect neighbor properties.

    neighbor_types : torch.Tensor
        Neighbor type indices, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, max_neighbors].
        Corresponds to neighbor_indices, giving type of each neighbor.

    neighbor_vectors : torch.Tensor
        Relative positions, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, max_neighbors, 4].
        Format: [distance, dx, dy, dz]
        - distance: ||r_j - r_i|| in Angstroms
        - dx, dy, dz: components of r_j - r_i vector
        Use distance for radial functions, components for angular terms.

    n_ghost : int
        Number of ghost atoms (periodic images) in the system.
        Usually can be ignored unless doing specialized handling.

    Returns
    -------
    Dict[str, torch.Tensor]
        Dictionary with the following keys:

        **Required**:
        - 'Etot' : torch.Tensor, shape [batch_size, 1]
            Total energy for each configuration in the batch.
            Must be provided and have correct shape.

        - 'Ei' : torch.Tensor, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, 1]
            Per-atom energy contributions. Should sum to Etot.
            Must be provided and have correct shape.

        **Optional** (provide only if computing analytically):

        - 'Force' : torch.Tensor, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, 3]
            Atomic forces F = -dE/dr in Cartesian coordinates.
            If not provided, computed automatically via autograd.

        - 'virial' : torch.Tensor, shape [batch_size, 3, 3]
            Virial stress tensor. Only relevant if providing Force.

        - 'atomic_virial' : torch.Tensor, shape [batch_size, n_atoms, 9]
            Per-atom virial contributions (flattened 3x3 tensors).
    """
    return {'Etot': torch.tensor([0.0])}

docs.title: Param(input_dict)
docs.text:
Source code in abfml\param\param.py 
def __init__(self, input_dict: dict):
    self.input_dict_new = {}
    global_dict = input_dict['global_setting']
    validator = DefaultValidatingDraft7Validator(global_set_schema)
    validator.validate(global_dict)
    self.GlobalSet = GlobalSet(**global_dict)
    if isinstance(self.GlobalSet.neighbor, list):
        self.GlobalSet.neighbor = {t: n for t, n in zip(self.GlobalSet.type_map, self.GlobalSet.neighbor)}

    data_dict = input_dict['data_setting']
    validator = DefaultValidatingDraft7Validator(data_set_schema)
    validator.validate(data_dict)
    self.DataSet = DataSet(**data_dict)

    train_dict = input_dict['train_setting']
    validator = DefaultValidatingDraft7Validator(train_set_schema)
    validator.validate(train_dict)
    self.TrainSet = TrainSet(**train_dict)

    loss_dict = input_dict['loss_setting']
    validator = DefaultValidatingDraft7Validator(loss_set_schema)
    validator.validate(loss_dict)
    self.LossSet = LossSet(**loss_dict)

    learning_rate_dict = input_dict['learning_rate']
    validator = DefaultValidatingDraft7Validator(learning_rate_schema)
    validator.validate(learning_rate_dict)
    self.LrSet = LrSet(**learning_rate_dict)

    self.model_name = input_dict['model_setting']['name']
    if input_dict['model_setting']['name'] in ['dp_se_e2_a', 'dp_se_e2_r', 'dp_se_e3']:
        fitting_config = input_dict['model_setting']['fitting_net']
        embedding_config = input_dict['model_setting']['descriptor']
        self.DeepSe = DeepSe(fitting_config=fitting_config, embedding_config=embedding_config)
    elif input_dict['model_setting']['name'] == 'BPMlp':
        fitting_config = input_dict['model_setting']['fitting_net']
        feature_config = input_dict['model_setting']['descriptor']
        self.BPDescriptor = BPDescriptor(fitting_config=fitting_config, feature_config=feature_config)
    elif input_dict['model_setting']['name'] == "NEP":
        fitting_config = input_dict['model_setting']['fitting_net']
        feature_config = input_dict['model_setting']['descriptor']
        self.NEPParam = NEPParam(fitting_config=fitting_config, feature_config=feature_config)
    elif input_dict['model_setting']['name'] == "test":
        self.test = self.Test(input_dict["model_setting"])
    elif input_dict['model_setting']['name'] == "user_defined":
        self.user_defined = self.UserDefined(input_dict["model_setting"])

    else:
        raise Exception(f"Undefined keyword: , Please read the manual!")

docs.title: derive_mechanics(grad_Ei, neighbor_vectors, neighbor_indices, n_ghost)
docs.text:
Source code in abfml\core\model\math_fun.py 
def derive_mechanics(
    grad_Ei: torch.Tensor,
    neighbor_vectors: torch.Tensor,
    neighbor_indices: torch.Tensor,
    n_ghost: int
) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    batch, n_atoms, max_neighbors = neighbor_indices.shape
    dtype, device = neighbor_vectors.dtype, neighbor_vectors.device

    # Initialize force and per-atom virial tensors
    force = torch.zeros(batch, n_atoms + n_ghost, 3, dtype=dtype, device=device)
    force[:, :n_atoms, :] = grad_Ei.sum(dim=-2)  # Direct contribution from central atoms

    atomic_virial = torch.zeros(batch, n_atoms + n_ghost, 9, dtype=dtype, device=device)

    # Extract relative position vectors (exclude norm)
    rel_pos = neighbor_vectors[..., 1:]  # Shape: [batch, n_atoms, max_neighbors, 3]

    # Compute local virial contributions via outer product of dr and dE
    local_virials = torch.matmul(rel_pos.unsqueeze(-1), -1 * grad_Ei.unsqueeze(-2)).reshape(batch, n_atoms, max_neighbors, 9)

    # Replace invalid neighbor indices (-1) with 0
    neighbor_indices[neighbor_indices == -1] = 0

    for b in range(batch):
        # Flatten indices and contribution values
        neighbor_idx_b = neighbor_indices[b].view(-1).to(torch.int64)

        # Force scatter-add
        force_contrib_b = -1 * grad_Ei[b].view(-1, 3)
        index_f = neighbor_idx_b.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, 3)
        force[b] = force[b].scatter_add(0, index_f, force_contrib_b)

        # Virial scatter-add
        virial_contrib_b = local_virials[b].view(-1, 9)
        index_v = neighbor_idx_b.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, 9)
        atomic_virial[b] = atomic_virial[b].scatter_add(0, index_v, virial_contrib_b)

    # Compute total virial by summing over all atoms
    virial = atomic_virial.sum(dim=1)

    return force, virial, atomic_virial

docs.title: ABFML Tutorials
docs.text: Welcome to ABFML — a machine learning force field (MLFF) framework based on PyTorch.

docs.title: 1. Train model
docs.text:
This tutorial section introduces three representative examples, each demonstrating a distinct use case of ABFML:

Build and fit a simple Lennard–Jones-like potential using ABFML’s modular interface

Example Description Mg–Cu Train a Deep Potential–Smooth Edition model for Mg–Cu alloy systems FCC–Au Learn to train a Behler–Parrinello type neural network model for pure Cu Custom Model Build and fit a simple Lennard–Jones-like potential using ABFML’s modular interface

💡 Tip

All tutorials can be found in the examples/ directory of the ABFML GitHub repository. Each includes ready-to-run scripts and datasets.

docs.title: 3. Running Simulations in LAMMPS and ASE
docs.text:
Once the model is trained, you can integrate it into LAMMPS for large-scale atomistic simulations.

This section covers: - Exporting ABFML-trained models to LAMMPS format - Setting up pair_style abfml and simulation input scripts - Running MD simulations with MLFFs

ABFML provides seamless integration with ASE (Atomic Simulation Environment) for structure optimization, NEB, and MD simulations.

Topics include: - Loading trained ABFML models into ASE calculators - Running energy/force evaluations - Performing relaxation and trajectory analysis

➡️ See: Using ABFML with ASE

docs.text:
ABFML also offers several useful utilities to assist your workflow: - Dataset preparation and splitting - Log parsing and visualization - Model inspection and export

docs.title: 6. Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
A typical ABFML workflow looks like this:

```mermaid graph LR A[Prepare Dataset] --> B[Configure input.json] B --> C[Train Model with ABFML] C --> D[Validate Results] D --> E[Export to LAMMPS/ASE] E --> F[Run Simulations]

docs.title: 1. Prepare the Dataset
docs.text:
Prepare a dataset containing total energy, atomic forces, and Virial tensors from DFT calculations.

  • Example dataset path: ../data/test.extxyz

docs.title: 2. Parameter Configuration
docs.text:
Create a file named input.json with the following content:

{
  "name": "model_parameters",
  "global_setting": {
    "type_map":[29],
    "neighbor": [100],
    "cutoff": 6.0,
    "dtype": "float64",
    "logger_file": "mlff.log"
  },
  "model_setting": {
    "name": "dp_se_e2_a",
    "descriptor": {
      "R_max": 6.0,
      "R_min": 0.5,
      "smooth_fun": "poly2_r",
      "network_size": [25,50,100],
      "bias": true,
      "resnet_dt": false,
      "activate_function": "tanh",
      "M2": 16
    },
    "fitting_net": {
      "network_size": [200,200,200],
      "bias": true,
      "resnet_dt": true,
      "activate_function": "tanh"
    }
  },
  "data_setting": {
    "file_format": "extxyz",
    "shuffle": true,
    "train_file":  ["../data/test.extxyz"],
    "valid_file":  ["../data/test.extxyz"]
  },
  "train_setting": {
    "epoch": 1,
    "optimizer":"Adam",
    "save_check": 5,
    "batch_size": 1,
    "print_freq": 1,
    "model_file": "model.pt"
  },
  "loss_setting": {
    "start_energy_weight": 1.0,
    "limit_energy_weight": 10.0,
    "start_force_weight": 100.0,
    "limit_force_weight": 10.0,
    "start_virial_weight": 1.0,
    "limit_virial_weight": 1.0,
    "start_ei_weight": 0.0,
    "limit_ei_weight": 0.0,
    "loss_file": "loss.curve"
  },
  "learning_rate": {
    "type_name": "exp",
    "decay_step": 500,
    "decay_rate": 0.95,
    "start_lr": 1.0e-3,
    "limit_lr": 1.0e-6
  }
}

🔹 Notes:

  • type_map: 29 corresponds to Cu. Modify according to your atomic types.
  • neighbor: Maximum number of neighbors considered per atom.
  • descriptor: Descriptor settings affecting local atomic environment representation.
  • fitting_net: Fitting network parameters.
  • loss_setting: Weights for energy, forces, and Virial; can change during training.
  • learning_rate: Exponential decay learning rate.

docs.title: Results Analysis
docs.text: In this section, we analyze the performance of the trained machine learning force field (MLFF) model through several key visualization methods. These plots provide intuitive insights into model convergence, accuracy, and error distribution, which are critical for evaluating and improving MLFF models.

docs.title: 1. Convergence Curve
docs.text:
The convergence curve shows how the total loss (and its components such as energy and force loss) evolve during training. It reflects whether the training process is stable and if the model parameters are converging properly.

Purpose in MLFF training:

  • Monitor model stability and overfitting.
  • Evaluate the balance between energy and force fitting.
  • Determine whether more epochs or different learning rate schedules are needed.

Example plot:

docs.title: 2. Parity Plot
docs.text:
The parity (diagonal) plot compares the predicted values (energy or force) with the reference DFT values. Each point represents one structure (for energy) or one atomic component (for force).

Purpose in MLFF training:

  • Visualize how well the MLFF reproduces DFT data.
  • Identify systematic bias (if points deviate from the diagonal).
  • Quantify the root-mean-square error (RMSE) and correlation (R²).

Example plot:

docs.title: 3. Error Distribution Plot
docs.text:
The error distribution (histogram) shows how the prediction errors (ΔE = E_pred − E_ref or ΔF = F_pred − F_ref) are distributed. A narrow, symmetric distribution centered around zero indicates a well-fitted and unbiased model.

Purpose in MLFF training:

  • Identify systematic over- or underestimation.
  • Evaluate uncertainty and variance in model predictions.
  • Compare model performance across datasets or architectures.

Example plot:

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Plot Type Description Insight Provided Convergence Curve Tracks loss over training steps Convergence stability, overfitting detection Parity Plot Compares MLFF vs DFT predictions Accuracy and bias visualization Error Distribution Histogram of prediction errors Spread and symmetry of model performance

These plots together form a comprehensive evaluation toolkit for MLFF model training and validation. They help researchers quickly identify performance bottlenecks and optimize model hyperparameters for better accuracy and transferability.
